set.explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is LV systolic dysfunction (EF below 45%) arising in late pregnancy or within 5 months of delivery, without another cause. About half of patients recover normal LV function, usually within 6 months, and it is treated like other forms of HFrEF (postpartum ACE inhibitors are safe; bromocriptine is considered). Recurrence in a later pregnancy is common, especially if LV function has not normalised, so future pregnancy needs specialist counselling; diagnosis does not require biopsy.

topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: A patient with HFrEF (EF 25%) who remains in NYHA III despite an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and diuretic should have a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist added (RALES), with potassium and renal monitoring; an SGLT2 inhibitor and switching to sacubitril/valsartan are further steps. Hydralazine–nitrate is reserved for intolerance of RAAS blockers or for self-identified Black patients who are still symptomatic. Aspirin, warfarin and amlodipine do not improve heart failure outcomes.

Multiply transfused patients (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia) develop secondary haemochromatosis, which causes diabetes, conduction disease and a cardiomyopathy (initially restrictive, later dilated) with low-voltage ECG. Iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation) are the first test, followed by cardiac MRI T2* to quantify myocardial iron; early chelation can reverse the cardiomyopathy. BNP only confirms heart failure without explaining it.

set.explanation: Natriuretic peptides have a high negative predictive value: a BNP below 100 pg/mL (NT-proBNP below 300 pg/mL in the acute setting) makes acute heart failure unlikely, so another cause of her breathlessness should be sought. A low BNP does not specifically point to PE, and a single borderline value cannot be interpreted by an arbitrary repeat threshold.

BNP is a counter-regulatory hormone: it causes natriuresis and diuresis, vasodilatation (including of the coronary and pulmonary vessels) and inhibition of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and sympathetic systems. Sacubitril raises natriuretic peptide levels by inhibiting neprilysin, which is part of how sacubitril/valsartan works.

BNP (with its inactive fragment NT-proBNP) is secreted mainly by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stretch, whereas ANP comes mainly from the atria. Levels rise in heart failure, ischaemia, valve disease, AF, pulmonary hypertension and renal failure, and fall with diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and in obesity.

Natriuretic peptides can be raised without LV failure in COPD (hypoxaemia and right ventricular strain), pulmonary embolism, AF, LVH, ischaemia, sepsis, renal impairment (eGFR below 60), cirrhosis and age over 70. Obesity and treatment with diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers or MRAs can lower levels and give false reassurance.
